en: Now then, Saegusa-sensei. If you would start the lesson.

All right. Well, Sawamura-san, it looks like you're the only
one here, but let's begin, shall we?
We'll begin with a lesson on proper language usage.

As you know, many people are guilty of misusing language in
their everyday lives.

Of course, this doesn't pose much of a problem when speaking
to friends or family, but it won't do for an announcer
speaking on national TV.

How embarrassing would it be to make a mistake when
speaking in front of millions?
That would be embarrassing, wouldn't it?

This brings us to your first problem to consider. I will
give you three sentences. You tell me which of them
contains a mistake.
So I choose the sentence that is incorrect?
Precisely. Here we go!
(Hmm. Which sentence has a mistake in it?)

I think number one, "He is just as tall as Alyssa and I," is
incorrect.

Oh, too bad! That one is correct. Some people say "as tall
as me," but "as" is a conjunction, and pronoun forms have to
match on either side.
Right. "He" is the subjective case of the pronoun, so "I" must also be the subjective case when making this comparison using "as."

The one that is incorrect is number two, "Alyssa and me did
our homework together."
What's incorrect about it?

Well, the people who did their homework are the subject of
the sentence, so the pronoun should be in subjective form:
i.e., "I," not "me."

Oh, I see! You do hear that kind of thing quite a lot,
though, don't you?

Yes, it's commonly used and readily understood but still
incorrect nonetheless.
Let's continue on to the next problem, shall we?

I think number two, "Alyssa and me did our homework
together," is incorrect.
That's correct! Very good, Sawamura-san!
Well! You're quite good at this, aren't you?
I don't think that one was all that difficult...

Perhaps, but I believe a lot of people wouldn't have known
the answer.

Indeed. The people who did their homework are the subject of
the sentence, so the pronoun should be in subjective form:
i.e., "I," not "me."
But you do hear that kind of thing quite a lot, though, don't you?

I think number three, "This is as good as it gets for Alyssa
and me," is incorrect.

Oh, too bad! That one is correct. Some people might say "for
Alyssa and I," but "for" is a preposition, so the pronoun should be objective.
Oh, I see! "Me" is an object of the preposition.

Oh, I see! You do hear that kind of thing a lot, though,
don't you?

Now, then. Which one of these three sentences contains a
mistake?

I think number one, "I literally cried for an hour," is
incorrect.

No, that one is fine. Many people do tend to use "literally"
incorrectly, however, when something isn't the actual,
literal truth.
For example, "I literally cried my eyes out," when, of course, they really didn't.

The one that is incorrect is number three, "If I'd known, I
would of done it differently."

Well, it should be "would have," not "would of." People do
misinterpret "would have" as "would of" fairly often in
colloquial speech, but they are in fact incorrect.
Yes, I do hear those a lot.
Hehe. Interesting, isn't it? Let's keep going, shall we?

I think number two, "I will do it regardless of the cost,"
is incorrect.

No, that one is fine. The one that is incorrect is number
three, "If I'd known, I would of done it differently."

I think number three, "If I'd known, I would of done it
differently," is incorrect.
Wonderful! You are correct!
Oh, I'm so glad!

Saegusa-sensei, could you please explain what the mistake
is? I'm afraid I'm not sure, myself.

Fujimoto-san, I'm appalled! How can you claim to represent
our school with such a shaky understanding of the language?
Please forgive me!

It should be "would have," not "would of." People do
misinterpret "would have" as "would of" fairly often in
colloquial speech, but they are in fact incorrect.

I think number one, "I accidently took the wrong bus," is
incorrect.
I see. And what makes you say that?
It should be "accidentally," not "accidently."
You're exactly right! I'm very impressed, Sawamura-san!

Well, that's enough of an introduction to proper language
usage. There are other skills that need to be cultivated as
well for voice-related work.

I think number two, "He made a complete 180-degree
turnabout," is incorrect.

I think number three, "I love fruit⑬e.g., bananas and
grapes," is incorrect.

No, actually, that one is fine. The one that is incorrect is
number one, "I accidently took the wrong bus."
Really? What's wrong with that one?
My goodness! I didn't even notice that.

Yes. Proper language use is a difficult thing, which is why
our course comes so highly recommended. I do hope you'll
consider enrolling.

(Hmm. I only came because she said it was free, but I guess
they're going to try and persuade me to sign up.)

But you are a very bright student of proper language usage,
aren't you? You got all of the problems correct, after all!

Hmm. Yes. I'm starting to worry there isn't much we can
teach you here.
But Saegusa-sensei! Surely there must be something else!

Ahem! No, you're right, of course. There is plenty more to
learn! Plenty! Let's move on to a new topic, shall we?

Now, through the use of tongue twisters, we'll practice
speaking rapidly yet clearly, an essential skill for any announcer!

That said, Sawamura-san, you did very well indeed! You got
most of the problems correct!

But what do you think so far, Sawamura-san? Our course is
packed full with useful information, wouldn't you agree?
Er⑬ Yes, of course.

I sincerely hope you'll enroll and continue studying with
us!

Now don't get ahead of yourself, Saegusa-sensei! The class
isn't over just yet!

Right! Now, through the use of tongue twisters, we'll
practice being able to speak rapidly yet clearly, an
essential skill for any announcer!
Tongue twisters?

That's right. Clear enunciation and fluency are essential
for any voice-related career!

Are you ready to start? I'll give you a tongue twister, and
you'll say it as fast as you can.

We'll start with one of the more common tongue twisters,
"She sells seashells."
She sells seasnells by the seashore!
She sells seashells by the seasnore!

No, I'm afraid that's incorrect. It's "She sells seashells
by the seashore," isn't that right?
Yes, I'm afraid I got a little tongue-tied.

Don't you worry, Sawamura-san! Keep practicing and study
hard, and you'll get there!

Fujimoto-san is right. Now, let's try a different tongue
twister, shall we?
Um, let's see...

Too slow! I'm afraid you took much too long, Sawamura-san.
The point is to say it as quickly as you can.
Yes, perhaps I was being too careful.
She sells seashells by the seashore!
Very good! Now, say it again!
Great! One more time!
That was perfect! You're quite a fluent speaker!

That one was just a warmup, however. On to the next tongue
twister!

This next one is also fairly well-known. It's the one about
"Peter Piper."
Peter Piper pecked a pick of pickled peppers!
Peter Piper picked a peck of peckled pippers!

Nope, sorry. It's supposed to be "Peter Piper picked a peck
of pickled peppers."
Wow, it's more difficult than I thought it would be.

That's all right! You can't be expected to do everything
perfectly right from the start! That's what training is for.

Still, this last one is going to be quite difficult. Are you
sure you're ready?

Too slow! I'm afraid you took much too long, Miss Sawamura.
Don't worry about making a mistake. Just go for it!
Okay, I'll try.
Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers!
Great! Say it one last time!
You did it, Sawamura-san! Well done!
That was amazing!

Now, this last one should prove quite difficult. Are you
sure you're ready?

And now for the big finish! This one is a little less
common. Have you heard it before?
It goes, "Many an anemone sees an enemy anemone." And please note that it's pronounced "uh-NEM-uh-nee."

Anemone? Those colorful sea creatures with the tentacles,
right? "Many an anemone sees an enemy anemone." Okay. I'll
do my best!
Many a nemone sees a nenemy nemone!
"Many a nemone"? That wasn't quite right, was it?
Many an enemy sees an anemone enemy!
"Many an enemy"? That wasn't quite right, was it?
Hmm. That one is really hard!

Not to worry! You'd have to be a professional to have this
one come easily. It takes training, and that's what we're
here for.
That was too slow, I'm afraid, Sawamura-san.
Many an anemone sees an enemy anemone!

I can't believe it! You got it exactly right! That was
incredible, Sawamura-san!
I can't believe it, either!
Ooh, I'm so happy!

I'm very impressed! You must have a natural aptitude for
this sort of thing.

That concludes our introductory class. Thank you very much
for coming today.
Thank you for such an interesting lesson!

Well... I really wanted to recommend that you enroll in our
school...

Nevertheless, Sawamura-san, it would seem you got all of our
practice problems perfectly correct.

I'm afraid you've left me without a way to persuade you to
join.

And after Saegusa-sensei gave you this introductory
lesson for free and everything!

I'm sorry, Ms. Fujimoto, but I'm afraid there's really
nothing left for me to teach Sawamura-san.

Next time, I hope you can bring me a student who requires
a bit more help.
Yes, I'll do my best.

(Aw, they seem like such nice people. I feel kind of guilty,
but at least now I can have confidence in my speaking
skills!)

You already possess some solid skills, but enrolling in our
school will help you refine them. Have you any interest in
being an announcer?

What do you say, Miss Sawamura? What a wonderful career that
would be!

(I really don't have the time for that right now. I only
took the class because it was free.)
I know what you're thinking. Your life is so busy already, and you just don't have the time.

Yes, I'm afraid that's true. I'm sorry, but I can't enroll
in your school...

Not to worry! We also have a home-study kit for busy
students like you. You can train in your spare time at home!

The kit includes a textbook on proper language usage, and an
anthology of one thousand tongue twisters as well! They can
be yours for only 500,000 yen!

At least, that's the usual price. But because you already
have such a solid foundation, we would like to give you a
discounted price of only 490,000 yen!
I'm afraid that, if you truly are interested in a voice-related career, you would need quite a bit of training here at our school first.

I'm sure you could tell from the introductory class that you
have many areas of weakness.

But don't you worry, Sawamura-san! We can help you! We'll
support you every step of the way as you work toward your dreams!
But, I...

At least, that's the usual price. But because you already
have some foundation, we would give you a discounted price
of only 490,000 yen!

Oh, no, Saegusa-sensei! Are you sure? That's far too much
of a discount for these wonderful materials!

Yes, well, Miss Sawamura is truly special. She deserves the
opportunity! What do you say, Miss Sawamura? Don't let this
chance slip away!
But I don't have that kind of money.

Think of it as an investment in your future! It may seem like a
lot of money now, but the return will be well worth it!

Both me and Fujimoto-san think that, with these materials,
you will learn the proper use of the language and gain
confidence in your skills!

"Me and Fujimoto-san think"? I thought you said that's
incorrect. Shouldn't it be "Fujimoto-san and I think"?
Saegusa-sensei! What were you thinking!?

I'm sorry, but I don't have that kind of money. I'm afraid I
won't be buying your study kit.
But they really are wonderful materials, well worth the price.

Do they contain example sentences such as "Me and
Fujimoto-san think"?

Oh, uh, well, that was just a simple slip of the tongue on
my part.

I'm sorry, but I'm afraid I have to be going now. I really
did enjoy the lesson, though. Thank you very much for your
time!
Darn. I really thought we had her...

Wait, what!? All these guys... By yourself? Screw this, I'm
outta here!
You're amazing, Akiyama-san.
Heh. You all right?
I'm so glad you were my manager today, Akiyama-san.
But now this really is the end, isn't it?
Yeah. That's how it goes.

I get to meet all kinds of people in this job, but things
tend to move so quickly, I usually never see them again.
